steps.hint: Double the force as well as the distance.

steps: Choose the equation: weight, work done, spring force, or elastic energy.
Convert units first: extension cm to m (divide by 100), and find weight before work done when lifting.
State the answer with its unit (N, J, N/m).
method_card.title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
method_card.content:
Four equations live here. Three are recall: weight \(W = mg\), work done \(W = Fs\), and spring force \(F = ke\). One is usually given: elastic energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) (check whether your board supplies it).

Weight is a force in newtons, so it often becomes the force in a work-done sum. Work done needs the distance moved in the direction of the force, so against gravity use the height. Extension is the change in length (stretched minus natural), converted to metres.

steps: Multi-step problems link equations: weight, then work done, then power \(P = W_d ÷ t\).
Elastic energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) squares the extension, so doubling the stretch stores four times the energy.
Watch for distractors: work against gravity uses only the vertical height, and a resultant force subtracts friction first.
gold.title: Gold: chain equations or square the extension

example.question: A hoist lifts a 50 kg load 6 m in 20 s. Calculate the power. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Pick the right equation: weight \(W = mg\), work done \(W = Fs\), or spring force \(F = ke\).
Write it, substitute the numbers, and multiply. In bronze the values are already in kg, N and m.
State the answer with its unit: N for force and weight, J for work, N/m for a spring constant.

example.question: A bag has a mass of 5 kg. Calculate its weight. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Same equations, but tidy the numbers first. Extensions in cm must become metres: divide by 100.
Lifting? Find the weight with \(W = mg\), then use that weight as the force in \(W = Fs\).
Rearranging \(F = ke\) for k gives \(k = F ÷ e\). Substitute only after the units are right.

exam_context.frequency: Very high: weight and work done appear almost every year, and springs link to required practicals.

gold.hint: Weight, then work done, then divide by the time.
gold.display: A person of mass 65 kg walks up 12 m of stairs in 15 seconds. Calculate the power they develop. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Three steps: weight, then work done climbing, then power.
Power is work done per second: \(P = W_d ÷ t\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the work done by the time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 7644 J, so P = 509.6 W is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply power by time to get work done.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: 65 × 9.8 = 637 N. Work done = 7644 J, power = 509.6 W. Using the mass as the force (65 × 12 ÷ 15 = 52) skips the weight.

gold.hint: Find the extension, convert to metres, square it, then half k e squared.
gold.display: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 8 cm to 20 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

guided_steps.say: Elastic potential energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\). Find the extension, convert to metres, then square.
Now substitute into \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\).

guided_steps.done: Back to e² = 0.0144, so Eₑ = 1.44 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100 (which is ½ × 200) to recover e².

misconceptions.message: Extension is the change: 20 − 8 = 12 cm = 0.12 m, not the full 20 cm. Using 0.20 m gives ½ × 200 × 0.04 = 4 J.
Square the extension: 0.12² = 0.0144. Forgetting to square (½ × 200 × 0.12) gives 12 J.

gold.hint: Rearrange to k = 2E divided by e squared.
gold.display: A spring stores 0.72 J of elastic PE when extended by 0.06 m. Calculate the spring constant.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) for k: \(k = 2E_e ÷ e^2\).
Now divide.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the doubled energy by e².

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.72 J, so k = 400 N/m is right.

misconceptions.message: Rearranging ½ke² for k gives k = 2E ÷ e². Forgetting the 2 (0.72 ÷ 0.0036) gives 200, half the real value.
e is squared: 0.06² = 0.0036. Using 0.06 instead (1.44 ÷ 0.06) gives 24.

gold.hint: Subtract friction to get the resultant force, then multiply by distance.
gold.display: A box of mass 40 kg is pushed 5 m across a rough floor by a force of 300 N. The friction force is 120 N. Calculate the resultant work done on the box.

guided_steps.say: The box feels two forces. Find the resultant first, then \(W = Fs\). The mass is not needed.

guided_steps.hint: Take friction from the pushing force.

guided_steps.say: Now \(W = Fs\) with the resultant force.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 180 N resultant, so W = 900 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Use the resultant force, not just the applied force. Resultant = 300 − 120 = 180 N, so W = 180 × 5 = 900 J. Using 300 gives 1500 J.
The mass (40 kg) is a distractor here. Work done needs a force and a distance, not the mass.

gold.hint: Elastic energy equals kinetic energy; solve for v.
gold.display: A spring with spring constant 50 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. The stored energy is transferred to a 0.02 kg ball. Assuming all elastic PE converts to kinetic energy, calculate the speed of the ball.

guided_steps.say: Two energy stores. First the elastic PE, then set it equal to the kinetic energy.
All of this becomes kinetic energy: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.25\). Rearrange: \(v^2 = 2E ÷ m\).

guided_steps.hint: Double the energy, divide by the mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.25 J, so v = 5 m/s is right.

misconceptions.message: Elastic PE = ½ × 50 × 0.1² = 0.25 J. Set equal to KE: ½ × 0.02 × v² = 0.25, so v² = 25 and v = 5 m/s.
Square the compression: 0.1² = 0.01, giving Eₑ = 0.25 J.

gold.hint: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height.
gold.display: A crane lifts a 350 kg beam 8 m and also moves it 15 m horizontally. Calculate the total work done by the crane against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height. First the weight, then \(W = Fs\) with the height.
Lift the weight through the vertical height of 8 m. The 15 m sideways does no work against gravity.

guided_steps.hint: Weight times the vertical height only.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 3430 N weight, so 27,440 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the height to recover the weight.

misconceptions.message: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height. Weight = 3430 N, so W = 3430 × 8 = 27,440 J. Adding the 15 m sideways (using 23 m) gives 78,890 J.
Gravity is a vertical force, so only the vertical height matters. The horizontal 15 m is a distractor.

bronze.hint: Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.
bronze.display: A book has a mass of 1.5 kg. Calculate its weight. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Weight is a force: \(W = mg\), mass times gravitational field strength.

guided_steps.hint: The mass is already given in kilograms.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 1.5 kg, so W = 14.7 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the weight by g to get the mass.

misconceptions.note: gave the mass instead of the weight
misconceptions.message: Weight is a force in newtons, not the mass. Multiply: W = 1.5 × 9.8 = 14.7 N.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A force of 200 N is used to push a box 6 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is \(W = Fs\): force times distance moved.

guided_steps.hint: The force is given in newtons.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 N, so W = 1200 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the work by the distance.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 200 × 6 = 1200 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply the spring constant by the extension.
bronze.display: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m and is extended by 0.2 m. Calculate the force on the spring.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law: \(F = ke\), spring constant times extension.
Substitute into \(F = ke\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.2 m, so F = 5 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide force by k to get the extension.

misconceptions.message: F = k × e, so multiply: 25 × 0.2 = 5 N. Dividing k by e (giving 125) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Use the Moon's g value, not Earth's.
bronze.display: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. Calculate their weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg.

guided_steps.say: Weight \(W = mg\). Use the Moon's gravitational field strength, not Earth's.
Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to g = 1.6, so W = 128 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide weight by mass to get g.

misconceptions.message: Use the Moon's g = 1.6, not Earth's 9.8. W = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N. Using 9.8 gives 784 N.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A dog pulls a sled with a force of 150 N over a distance of 20 m. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is \(W = Fs\): force times distance moved.

guided_steps.hint: The force is given in newtons.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 150 N, so W = 3000 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the work by the distance.

misconceptions.message: Work done = F × s = 150 × 20 = 3000 J.

bronze.hint: Find the extension, convert it to metres, then divide the force by it.
bronze.display: A spring has a natural length of 10 cm. When a 4 N force is applied, it stretches to 18 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law is \(F = ke\). You know F and the lengths, so find the extension, then rearrange for k.

guided_steps.hint: Take the natural length from the stretched length.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(F = ke\) to \(k = F ÷ e\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the force by the extension in metres.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4 N, so k = 50 N/m is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply k by extension to get the force.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m first: 8 cm = 0.08 m. k = 4 ÷ 0.08 = 50 N/m. Dividing by 8 gives 0.5, which is wrong.
Extension is the change in length, not the total length: 18 − 10 = 8 cm.

bronze.display: Which equation gives the weight of an object?

misconceptions.message: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg). W = Fs is work done, not weight. They share the letter W but mean different things.

bronze.hint: Weight is mass times g, in newtons.
bronze.display: A weightlifter raises a 60 kg barbell. Calculate the weight of the barbell. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Weight is a force: \(W = mg\), mass times gravitational field strength.

guided_steps.hint: The mass is already given in kilograms.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 60 kg, so W = 588.0 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the weight by g to get the mass.

misconceptions.note: gave the mass instead of the weight
misconceptions.message: Weight is a force in newtons, not the mass. W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.

silver.hint: Find the weight first, then use it as the force in work done.
silver.display: A crate of mass 25 kg is lifted 3 m onto a shelf. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Lifting: first find the weight, then use it as the force in \(W = Fs\).
That weight is the force you lift against. Now \(W_d = Fs\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the weight by the height.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 245 N weight, so 735 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: W = mg = 245 N. Then work done = 245 × 3 = 735 J. Using the mass directly (25 × 3 = 75) skips the weight step.

silver.hint: Extension is the change in length; convert cm to metres before substituting.
silver.display: A spring has a spring constant of 80 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 12 cm to 27 cm. Calculate the force applied.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law \(F = ke\). Find the extension, convert to metres, then substitute.
Substitute into \(F = ke\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.15 m, so F = 12 N is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m first: 15 cm = 0.15 m. F = 80 × 0.15 = 12 N. Using 15 gives 1200 N.
Use the extension (27 − 12 = 15 cm), not the total stretched length.

silver.hint: Weight, then work done, then divide by the time for power.
silver.display: A forklift lifts a 200 kg pallet 4 m in 10 seconds. Calculate the power of the forklift. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Three steps: weight, then work done, then power.
Power is work done per second: \(P = W_d ÷ t\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the work done by the time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 7840 J of work, so P = 784 W is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply power by time to get work done.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: 200 × 9.8 = 1960 N. Work done = 7840 J, power = 784 W. Using the mass as the force (200 × 4 ÷ 10 = 80) skips the weight.

silver.hint: Square the extension, then use half k e squared.
silver.display: A spring has a spring constant of 60 N/m and is stretched by 0.25 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.

guided_steps.say: Elastic potential energy uses \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\). Square the extension first.
Now substitute into \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\).

guided_steps.done: Back to e² = 0.0625, so Eₑ = 1.875 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Reverse the steps: ×2 then ÷60 recovers e².

misconceptions.message: Square the extension: 0.25² = 0.0625. Eₑ = ½ × 60 × 0.0625 = 1.875 J. Forgetting to square (½ × 60 × 0.25) gives 7.5 J.
Do not forget the ½. Eₑ = ½ × 60 × 0.0625 = 1.875 J. Leaving out the half gives 3.75 J.

silver.hint: Multiply force by distance, then convert joules to kilojoules.
silver.display: A friction force of 500 N acts on a car as it moves 80 m. Calculate the work done against friction in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Work done \(W = Fs\). The answer is asked in kilojoules, so convert at the end.

guided_steps.done: Back to 40,000 J, so 40 kJ is right.

misconceptions.note: forgot to convert J to kJ
misconceptions.message: W = 500 × 80 = 40,000 J. The question wants kilojoules: 40,000 ÷ 1000 = 40 kJ.

silver.hint: Convert one extension to metres, then divide its force by it.
silver.display: A spring is stretched by adding masses. With a 3 N load, the extension is 6 cm. With a 5 N load, the extension is 10 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.

guided_steps.say: \(F = ke\), so \(k = F ÷ e\). Use one pair, convert the extension to metres.

guided_steps.pre: Check with the other pair: 10 cm = 0.10 m, so 5 ÷ 0.10 =
guided_steps.done: Same k both times, so k = 50 N/m is right.
guided_steps.hint: The second pair should give the same k.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m before dividing: 6 cm = 0.06 m. k = 3 ÷ 0.06 = 50 N/m. Dividing by 6 gives 0.5.
Either data point works: 3 ÷ 0.06 = 50 and 5 ÷ 0.10 = 50 N/m.
